case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 11.02.1991 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Writ Petition No. 6 of 1991.)
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J : I have gone through the judgments written by my learned brothers ATM Afzal and Latifur Rahman, JJ. I agree with the decision of brother ATM Afzal J.

ATM Afzal, J : These two appeals by leave, CA 22/91 by the Collector of Customs and the Chairman, Board of Revenue, and CA 23/91 by the two auction-purchasers, arise out of the same judgment and order dated 11 February, 1991 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka making the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No 6 of 1991. Facts and law involved in the two appeals being the same, they have been heard analogously and will be disposed of by this judgment.

2. Respondent No. 1 Anis & Co. (in both the appeals) brought the aforesaid Writ Petition on 2.1.91 calling in question the letter dated 23.12.90 of the Collector of Customs(Annexure K to the Writ Petition) reiterating his refusal to grant clearance in respect of 5000 metric tons of Iraqi Ordinary Grey Portland Cement out of 10,000 metric tons awaiting delivery with a prayer to restrain the Collector from disposing of the said cement during the pendency of the Rule and further to direct him to deliver the same to the respondent upon obtaining proper guarantee. The appellants of C.A 22/91 were respectively made respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation was made respondent No. 3 in the said writ petition. The appellants of CA 23/91 were added as respondents Nos. 4 and 5. The respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 are respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 respectively in CA 22/91.

3. Respondent No. is case in the writ petition, briefly, was that M/s Transclear SA of Lausanne, Switzerland purchased 10,000 metric tons of cement as aforesaid from an Iraqi Company, ‘14 namely, Layth Mandi Saleh and sold the same in favour of M/s Nidera Hendels Compagnie of Holland for "cash against documents" and M/s Nidera sold the same to M/s MA Baker of Chittagong against irrevocable Letter of Credit in favour of M/s Nideraopened by the said M/s MA Baker through Grindlays Bank, Chittagong. The said Cement was loaded from the Port Umm Qasr, Iraq from 14.7.90 onwards on board the Ship MV Banglar Kiron belonging to the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation which was chartered by the State Enterprise for Water Transport, Baghdad. The original sale by M/s Transclear to M/s Nidera being in cash against documents, the Bill of Lading was issued by the charterer of the ship with the term "to the order of Transclear SA" as the consignee, but the Bill of Lading was not supplied to the importer and the notifying party was M/s MA Baker. The said cement arrived at the port of Chittagong on 24.7.90. The Bill of Entry was submitted by M/s MA Baker to the Customs Authority but as the said M/s MA Baker failed to submit the Bill of Lading in Original to the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation it had to furnish Indemnity Bond and took delivery of cement to the extent of 4000 metric tons only. Later on M/s MA Baker did not turn up to take delivery of the balance cement in spite of repeated calls.

4. A dispute was raised by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation claiming the balance charter fees which resulted in a money suit being Money Suit No. 387 of 1990 in the 2nd Court of the Sub-Judge, Chittagong. It was prayed by the Corporation to hold an auction sale of the balance quantity of cement on their claim of having a lien on the said cement but the Court refused to give any relief.

5. The respondent stated that since the ownership of the cement continued to remain with the document of title, i.e. the bill of lading lying with the said M/s Transclear and as the importer M/s MA Baker refused to take delivery of the remaining cement, M/s Transclear sold the said cement to the respondent, assigned the bills of lading in its favour and sent the same to its banker Agrani Bank through their banker, Credit Swiss. (copy of one such bills of lading is annexed to the writ petition as Annexure A). M/s Agrani Bank then applied for permission of the Bangladesh Bank for remittance of the price of the balance quantity of cement (US$ 1,25,000/00) to which the Bangladesh Bank agreed upon adding certain conditions allegedly at the influence of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation vide its letter dated 22.11.90 (Annexure D).

6. The respondent further alleged that the Chief Controller of Import and Export (CCI & E) was creating various obstacles at the instance of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation in getting the balance quantity of cement and so the respondent approached the Ministry of Commerce which informed that the permission of the CCI & E was not necessary as the import of cement was not restricted. The Customs Collector, however, in the meantime put the said cement to auction sale under section 82 of the Customs Act 1969 to which the respondent objected by serving notice. In reply to the notice, the Customs Collector informed that the goods had already been auctioned, but if the necessary formalities could be done before the approval of the bid, the respondent could yet get delivery of the same (Customs' letter dated 26.11.90 marked as Annexure H). The Customs authority, however, by their letter dated 13.12.90 (Annexure I) and finally by the impugned letter dated 23.12.90 (Annexure K) rejected the respondent's claim to the cement in question. The respondent alleged that the ownership of the cement passed with the bill of lading which had been endorsed in its favour and thus the rejection of its claim to and holding of auction of the cement in question by the Customs Authority were illegal and without jurisdiction.

7. The appellants (in CA 22.91) in their affidavit-in-opposition, inter alia, stated that M/s MA Baker submitted 5 (five) bills of Entry on 22.7.1990 for clearance of 10 consignments of cement imported against LC No. G/1502/2518/90 and these bills of entry were submitted along with other necessary documents like invoice, letter of credit, letter of credit authorisation (LCA) Insurance, Indent and copy of the bills of lading duly certified by the LC opening Bank viz ANZ Grindlays Bank, Chittagong as the original documents from the supplier were not received at the time of the submission of those bills of Entry. Those were accepted for Customs assessment and after paying the requisite customs duties and charges the importer cleared 4000 metric tons of cement with an undertaking to produce the original documents. Out of the bills of Entry submitted the importer paid duties and taxes against 2 bills of Entry on 24.7.1990 and cleared 4000 metric tons; the other bills of Entry were assessed by the officials of the Customs House, Chittagong but the importer did not pay the duties and charges and as such the consignments remained uncleared.

8. The Collector of Customs has no knowledge whether the supplier has sold the cement in question to the respondent nor M/s Baker informed about any change in the ownership nor the shipping Agent who submitted the Import General Manifest applied for any amendment or change in the same wherein the importer of the consignment was shown as M/s MA Baker.

9. It was stated that the respondent's claim without fulfilling the requirements of Customs law in respect of the balance amount of cement which was awaiting clearance could not be lawfully entertained. It was also stated that the importer M/s MA., Baker submitted the requisite import documents for taking clearance of the import consignments and those documents were found genuine and valid. The respondent's claim without cancellation of the original importer's Bills of Entry and clearance from the CCI & E, the Bangladesh Bank and the Shipping Agents could not be entertained. The respondent failed to produce such necessary papers and documents and hence its claim was rejected lawfully. The permission of CCI & E is necessary as they are the competent authority who can relieve the respondent from compliance with the requisite normal import procedures as the respondent neither have LCA nor opened LC importing the cement nor have any indent. M/s MA Baker have done all such formalities and the Invoice, Certificate of Origin of the goods, Bills of lading etc. were issued in their name and the Manifest(IGM) submitted by the shipping agent also contained the name of M/s MA. Baker as the importer but nowhere the name of the respondent was shown as importer and as such there was no legal scope for accepting the respondent to be the lawful importer.

10. It was stated that the Customs Authority had to take steps for disposal of the consignment through auction when the importer M/s MA Baker failed to clear the goods within the stipulated time as envisaged in section 82 of the Customs Act. The public auction was held on 20.12.1990 and the highest bid of Taka 92.50 lacs was approved by the Collector of Customs. The auction purchasers had already deposited the bid amount in the Government Treasury on 30.12.90 and lifted some quantity of cement prior to 2.1.91 when stay order was passed by the High Court Division and delivery of cement was stopped.

11. The Bangladesh Shipping Corporation in its affidavit-in-opposition joined issue with the respondent, denied the allegations made against it and laid its claim to the disputed cement on account of alleged lien on the cargo including charter hire and other charges and damages which is alleged to be the first' charge on the cargo after the payment of customs duty and port charges. It was stated that its ship carried the cement from Iraq under a charter party Agreement but the charter hire charge @ US Dollar 4000/00 per day remained unpaid since 28.7.90 upto the date of the release of the ship. M/s MA Baker took delivery of only 4000 metric tons and the balance remained uncleared for about 2-1/2 months when the charterer advised the Corporation to exercise lien on the cargo.

12. The balance quantity of the cement was ultimately unloaded and stored in the port shed under the custody of the Customs allegedly at the cost of the Shipping Corporation.

13. The auction purchasers of the disputed cement (appellants in CA 23/91) in their affidavits-in-opposition stated that they along with others purchased 5000 metric tons of cement through auction held on 20.12.90 at the instance of the Collector of Customs and paid the entire amount of Tk. 92/50 lacs by two instalments. They also paid Tk. 2,77,500/00 as Income Tax and Tk. 12000/00 as inventory charges. Until the stay order was passed by the High Court Division they took delivery of216 metric tons of cement out of 5000 tons.

14. During the pendency of the present appeals, on an application by the auction purchasers which was not opposed, they were permitted to take delivery of the remaining cement by order dated 28.3.91 but the sale proceeds were to be retained by the Collector, of Customs pending disposal of the appeals. It is stated in their additional paper book that between 20.4.91 and 29.4.91 they received 18586 bags of cement when the unprecedented cyclone and tidal bore hit on the night following 29.4.91 and the entire lot of cement (balance) went under tidal water. After starting of the normal function on 9.5.91 they took delivery of 39200 more bags raising the total to 62986 bags out of 110848 bags purchased in auction.

15. They have alleged that they reported the matter to the Collector of Customs on 28.5.91 and demanded refund of Tk. 41,19,003/72 being the price of the cement not supplied but no payment was made.

16. These are all the facts of the case till date.

17. The High Court Division found in the impugned judgment that the Collector of Customs acted without lawful authority in refusing to deliver the consignment in question to respondent No. 1 and in holding the auction sale thereof. Accordingly the Rule was made absolute and the Collector of Customs was directed to deliver the balance quantity of cement to the respondent on its furnishing an Indemnity Bond.

18. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division upon a correct appreciation of the relevant laws, particularly relating to importation of goods and functions of the Customs Authorities and the special facts of the present case was justified in making the finding as above.

19. It will be fair to acknowledge that the case involved consideration of difficult matters relating to international trade and trade practices and various mercantile instruments with their bearing on municipal laws i.e. laws regulating import and export, collection of customs duty, etc. For a generalist it may not be very easy to get to the correct facts and its implications without serious endeavour in that behalf and without a proper understanding of the relevant laws. In order to explain the legal basis of the respondent's claim as an endorsee on the bill of lading "to the order of Transclear SA", Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned counsel for respondent (No. 1) had to file an additional paper book containing various correspondences between the Bangladesh Bank and other banks and other documents including Uniform Rules for Collections issued by the International Chamber of Commerce, Paris, besides making reference to text books, authorities and decisions. The exercise was necessary, because, although not directly relevant for deciding the crucial question in the case, there was no reference to Transclear SA, the endorser of the respondent, in any of the documents including the copy of the bill of lading filed by M/s MA Baker, the original importer, to the Customs along with the Bill of Entry on the basis of which assessment of duty was made nor there was any reference in the documents filed by the shipping agent.

20. It seems, however, that the High Court Division felt no difficulty at all in declaring the title of the respondent by merely looking at the endorsement overleaf the bill of lading produced by it and giving the direction as above only on the basis thereof. We are appalled to notice the inept and incorrect expressions used in the discussion in the judgment, failure to grasp the facts of the case and the legal provisions and the sweeping remarks made without proper appreciation which have marred the entire judgment. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed frankly submitted that he cannot support all the reasonings and discussions in the impugned judgment but, nevertheless, the operative part of it is otherwise supportable.

21. In order to illustrate the observations made above as to the impugned judgment two instances out of many may be cited. At one place it has been stated.

"Therefore, the where question centres round the ownership of the cement in question as alleged by the respondent Nos. 1 and 3, but, in our view, these respondent Nos. 1 and 3 have no locus standi to question the bill of lading. Only the real owner can raise such question when the petitioner is in custody of the same with due endorsement therein. M/s Transclear, the consignee of M/s MA Baker, was the agent of M/s MA Baker and the consignee having sold the goods in favour of the petitioner forwarded the bill of lading in favour of the Banker of M/s MA Baker, the respondent No. 1 could accept the same. We do not find that the present petitioner is disentitled to clear up the goods in question subject to payment of levy and taxes as payable under the Customs law."

22. The High Court Division, it is clear, made no real endeavour to appreciate the legal effect of a transfer by endorsement in a bill of lading generally and its utility to the Customs Authority in the facts of the present case for giving clearance in respect of the balance of the cement in question. This subject will be dealt with briefly hereafter but to revert to the impugned judgment it will be seen that it was wrongly held that M/s Transclear was the consignee of M/s MA Baker or that M/s MA Baker was the agent of M/s Transclear. Except the respondent's own assertion made in the writ petition there is nothing to show that M/s Transclear sold the goods to the respondent. It is nobody's case that the bill of lading was forwarded by M/s Transclear to the Banker of M/s MA Baker. Even Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed did not contend that merely because the respondent had the bill of lading endorsed to it , it was entitled to clearance of the goods by simply producing the bill of lading and making payment of the customs duty, etc.

23. As to the efficacy of a bill of lading, however, Mr. Ahmed submitted that it is a document of title to the goods in question and the title passes to the endorsee of the same. The learned Additional Attorney-General and Mr. Nurullah, learned counsel for the appellants in CA 23/91 have, however, contended that the bill of lading merely represents the goods but the right of property in the goods depends upon the transaction between the parties independent of the bill of lading.

<u>24. In Charlesworth's Mercantile Law (Eleventh Edition) (Civil M. Schmitthoff David AG Sarre) at page 322 it has been stated that a bill of lading serves three purposes—</u>

<u>(1) It is a receipt for goods shipped, containing the terms on which they have been received.</u>

<u>(2) It is evidence of the contract for the carriage of the goods.</u>

<u>(3) It is a document of title to the goods specified therein.</u>

<u>Mr. Ahmed referred to British Shipping Laws Vol. 3: Carver's Carriage by Sea (Vol. 2) Twelfth Edition) which says at page 886;</u>

<u>1045-The right to have possession of the goods passes to the transferee of the bill of lading; that is the symbol of the goods, and a transfer of it is, symbolically, a transfer of the possession of the goods themselves. Until the goods have been delivered, a delivery of the duly endorsed bill of lading operates, as between the transferor and transferee, and all who claim through them, as a physical delivery of the goods would do. And thus the possession may, in effect, be passed from one buyer pledgee, etc. to another, while the goods are still in the hands of the shipowner.</u>

<u>The learned Additional Attorney-General, however, referred to the same book (Thirteenth Edition) Vol. 2, page 1139 which under the heading 'Effect of transfer of bill of lading says that:</u>

<u>1623-There have been great difference of opinion among learned Judges as to legal effect of a transfer of a bill of lading, duly endorsed, in regard to the vesting of the properly in the goods. On the one hand, the view appears to have been that where there has been a real transfer of the bill of lading, not mere handing to an agent, nor a possession obtained by a thief, the property in the goods, as well as the right to possession follows the bill of lading.</u>

<u>On the other hand, the view now established is that the bill of lading merely represents the goods, not the right to them; and that possession of it is only equivalent to a physical possession of them. The right of property in the goods depends upon the transaction between the parties, of which the transfer of the bill of lading mayor may not have been an accident.</u>

<u>Such a transfer indicates nothing more than a delivery of the goods would do. It may have accompanied a sale of the goods; or it may have been given to complete a pledge; or, again, merely to enable an agent to obtain delivery.</u>

<u>25. In Sewell Vs. Burdick (1884) LR (Vol X) App. Case 74 cited by the learned Additional Attorney-General, Lord Bramwell observed that the truth is that the property does not pass by the endorsement, but by the contract in pursuance of which the endorsement is made. Earl Selborne pointed out that every endorsement does not operate as passing of property. The true intent and operation of the endorsement has to be obtained so as to see whether the shipper still retains any proprietary right in the goods.</u>

26. Whether by the transaction by endorsement in a bill of lading the property in the goods passes or not may not be free from doubt but this much appears to be settled that an endorsee is at least entitled to the possession of the goods on the basis of a duly endorsed bill of lading. In the present case although the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has frontally challenged the authority of Mis Transclear to endorse the bill of lading to the respondent, it does not become necessary to examine the validity of the endorsement because the Customs Authority apparently did not reject the respondent's prayer raising any question as to its title of the goods in dispute. It has, however, already been noticed that in none of the documents filed by M/s MA Baker there was any reference to M/s Transclear. Even so we shall proceed to examine the matter on the basis that there was a valid endorsement in favour of the respondent which at least entitled it to the possession of the goods which Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed took pains to impress upon us. Mr. Ahmed, however, conceded that the shipping agent or the carrier could raise objection in making delivery of the goods to the respondent but that stage had not been reached.

27. The High Court Division proceeded on the simple assumption that when the goods had already been validly imported by M/s Baker, the Customs Authority could no longer insist on the production of the same documents and observance of the same formalities by the respondent over again as was required of the original importer and it was entitled to the clearance of the goods on the basis of its being an endorsee in the bill of lading more so, when there was no other claimant. It is true that much emphasis has been given by the appellants in their affidavit-in-opposition and arguments on the failure of the respondent to produce the valid import authorisation documents like an importer who or his agent alone can ordinarily claim the clearance of the goods. Upon hearing full arguments and going through the records, however, it is now clear that the main ground of objection; although raised by the appellants, was not properly focused in the High Court Division and not appreciated at all by the court.

28. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed wasted no time in submitting that the respondent does not even pretend to be the importer of the goods and although it claims to have become the owner subsequently the customs authority may not clear the goods in its favour notwithstanding the endorsement in the bill of lading unless they are satisfied that the substitution of the respondent in place of the original importer does not offend any law relating to import. In other words, clearance from the Bangladesh Bank showing that the respondent had necessary permission to remit the required foreign exchange for the goods and clearance from the import control authority waiving formalities already performed were necessary. Mr. Ahmed referred to the letter of the Bangladesh Bank dated 22.11.90 (Annexure D) and the letter from the Ministry of Commerce dated 2.12.90 (Annexure E) and vigorously submitted that the necessary clearance from the concerned authorities was there and, therefore, the customs had no valid ground to refuse clearance of the goods. We shall presently see that Mr. Ahmed's Contention that the necessary clearance was there cannot be sustained.

29. It may be recalled that the appellants specifically stated, inter alia, in their Affidavit-in-opposition that since M/s MA Baker submitted the Bill of Entry with all import documents, the respondent's claim could not be entertained without the permission of the Chief Controller of Imports & Exports, shortly the CCI & E, who is the competent authority to relieve the respondent from compliance with the requisite import procedures and further without the clearance from the Bangladesh Bank as the respondent neither opened any LC nor had LCA for the remaining cement. Admittedly the letter of credit was opened by M/s MA Baker for US$ 5,90,000 covering import in the entire 10,000 metric tons of cement through ANZ Grindlays Bank and the beneficiary thereof was M/s Nidera. The bill of Entry shows that the consignor was M/s Nidera; the certificate of origin, weighment list, packing list etc. were all furnished by M/s Nidera. In the copy of the bill of lading produced by M/s Baker it was written "to the order of Grindlays Bank, Chiuagong." Now the respondent's bill of lading sent to Agrani Bank . shows "to the Order of Transclear SA" and this change evidently needed fresh permission from the Bangladesh Bank for remittance of US.$ 1,25,000 (said to be the price for 5000 metric tons) which Mr. Ahmed does not dispute. Indeed the respondent's banker, Agrani Bank applied for such permission in reply to which Bangladesh Bank sent its letter dated 22.1l.90 which Mr. Ahmed wants us to treat as a clearance for remitting the foreign exchange. Bangladesh Bank in the said letter, which is crucial for a decision in this case stated thus:

<p align="center">বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক</p>

<p align="center">প্রধান কার্যালয়</p>

<p align="center">ডাক বাক্স-৩২৫</p>

<p align="center">ঢাকা।</p>

<p>সহকারী মহাব্যবস্থাপক,                      তারিখঃ ২২-১১-৯০ ইং।</p>

<p>অগ্রণী ব্যাংক,</p>

<p>রমনা শাখা, ঢাকা।</p>

প্রিয় মহোদয়,

গ্রীনল্যাজ ব্যাংক, চট্টগ্রাম কর্তৃক প্রতিষ্ঠিত জে ১৫০২/১০/১৫১৮ তারিখ ১৪-৭-৯০ নম্বর ঋণ পত্রের বিপরীতে আমদানীকৃত সিমেন্টের আংশিক মূল্য মেসার্স আনিস এন্ড কোং কর্তৃক পরিশোধের অনুমতির আবেদন প্রসংগে।

উপরোল্লেখিত বিষয়ে আপনাদের বৈই/নিঃইঃ/১২১৭/৯০ তারিখ ২৩-১০-৯০ পত্রের প্রতি দৃষ্টি আকর্ষন করা যাইতেছে।

গ্রীনল্যাজ ব্যাংক, চট্টগ্রাম এর শিরোনামে উল্লেখিত ঋণ পত্রের বিপরীতে আমদানীকৃত সিমেন্ট এর মধ্যে ৫০০০ মেঃ ট্রন সিমেন্ট (+%-১০) আমদানীকারক মেসার্স এম,এ,বাকার গ্রহণ করিতেছে না বিধায় উক্ত পরিমাণ সিমেন্ট মেসার্স আনিস এন্ড কোম্পানী গ্রহণ করিতে ইচ্ছুক। এবং উক্ত সিমেন্ট এর প্রাপ্ত মূল্য ১,২৫,০০০/- প্রকৃত সরবরাহকারী মেসার্স ট্রান্স ক্লিয়ার, সুইজারল্যান্ড বরাবরে প্রেরণ করিতে ইচ্ছুক বলিয়া আপনাদের উপরোক্ত পত্রে জানাইয়াছেন। কিন্তু মেসার্স এম,এ,বাকার কর্তৃক প্রতিষ্ঠিত ঋণ পত্রের বিপরীতে আমদানীকৃত মালামাল মেসার্স আনিস এন্ড কোম্পানী কর্তৃক গ্রহণ/ছাড়করণ প্রচলিত আমদানী নীতি আদেশ নির্দেশিত ব্যবস্থার সহিত সংগতিপূর্ণ নহে। এই জন্য প্রধান নিয়ন্ত্রক, আমদানী ও রপ্তানী দপ্তরের অনুমতি আবশ্যক।

এমতাবস্থায় সুইজারল্যান্ডের মেসার্স ট্রান্স ক্লিয়ার এর অনুকুলে বৈদেশিক মুদ্রা প্রেরণের অনুমতি প্রদানের বিষয়টি নিম্নোক্ত শর্তে বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক বিবেচনা করিবে।

১। মেসার্স আনিস এন্ড কোং কর্তৃক আলোচ্য সিমেন্ট গ্রহণ/ছাড়করণের জন্য যদি সিসিআই এন্ড ই অনমতি প্রদান করেন।

২। বাংলাদেশ শিপিং কর্পোরেশন,শুল্ক কতপক্ষ এবং বন্দর কর্তৃপক্ষ যদি অনাপত্তি জ্ঞাপন করেন।

৩। বিষয়টি সম্পর্কে কোন বিচারালয়ে যদি আদালতে বিচারাধীন না থাকে।

৪। বাংলাদেশ শিপিং কর্পোরেশন কর্তৃপক্ষ এবং বন্দর কর্তৃপক্ষ পাওনা মিটাইবার পর মার্কিন ডলার ১,২৫,০০০/- হইতে যাহা অবশিষ্ট থাকিবে সেই পরিমাণ বৈদেশিক মুদ্রা প্রেরণ যোগ্য হইতে এবং উহা ঐ ওয়েজ আর্নার মার্কেট হইতে সংগ্রহ করিতে হইবে।

৫। কাষ্টম কর্তৃপক্ষ কর্তৃক সত্যায়িত বিল অব এন্ট্রি দাখিল করিতে হইবে।

উপরোক্ত শর্ত সমূহ পালন পূর্বক উপরোক্ত অনুমতি পত্র/অনাপত্তিপত্র/প্রশাসন সংস্থা যথাসময়ে বৈবদেশিক মুদ্রা রেমিটেন্স অনুমতির জন্য বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংকের নিকট পুনরায় আবেদন করা যাইতে পারে।

30. It is absolutely clear from the above letter that the respondent was required to comply with a number of conditions including obtaining permission from the CCI & E before it could even apply for permission for remittance of foreign exchange. It is not the respondent's case that the conditions laid down by the Bangladesh Bank were illegal or that it complied with the said conditions. It is very important to remember that the letter of the Bangladesh Bank has not been challenged in the writ petition. Mr. Ahmed, however, submitted that CCI & E's permission was not necessary because the Ministry of Commerce in its letter dated 2.12.90 stated that cement was a freely importable item and no permission of the Government was required for its importation. This letter is of little help to the respondent because even in that letter it is clearly stated that:

আমদানীর জন্য আমদানী ক্ষেত্রে প্রযোজ্য সাধারন নিয়মাদি পালন ব্যাত্তিরেকে সরকারের কোন অনুমতির প্রয়োজন নাই।

The Ministry of Commerce does not appear to have been posted with the special facts of the case as was the Bangladesh Bank and as such the Bank's instructions as above must prevail. The Ministry merely gave an opinion as if in an ordinary case. Even so, its reference to the observance of ordinary rules of import necessarily brings in the question of clearance from the CCI & E as pointed out by the Bangladesh Bank. The Collector of Customs in the letter dated 13.12.90, inter alia, specifically raised the objection that the respondent had failed to obtain clearance from the CCI & E and the Bangladesh Bank and as such its prayer was rejected.

31. Chapters IX and X of the Customs Act 1969 relate to the "Discharge of Cargo and Entry inwards of goods" and "clearance of goods for home-consumption". The powers and functions of the Customs officials in connection therewith are clearly laid down therein.

Section 79 provides that the owner of any imported goods shall deliver to the appropriate officer a Bill of Entry in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct.

Section 80 provides that on the delivery of such bill, the goods or such part thereof as may be necessary may, without undue delay, be examined or tested, and thereafter the goods shall be assessed to duty, if any, and the owner of such goods may then proceed to clear the same for home-consumption or warehouse them, subject to the provisions hereinafter contained.

Section 83 provides that when the owner of any goods entered for home-consumption and assessed under section 80 has paid the import duty and other charges, if any in respect of the same, the appropriate officer, if he is satisfied that the import of the goods is not prohibited or in breach of any restrictions or conditions applying to the import of such goods, may make an order for the clearance of the same.

<u>32. In the present case it is admitted that M/s MA Baker submitted the bill of entry as the owner of the disputed cement and assessment of duty was made in respect of the entire amount of cement i.e. 10,000 metric tons. M/s Baker paid the import duty for 4,000 metric tons and lifted the same. The respondent then comes in and asks for clearance of 5000 metric tons of cement evidently as the substituted owner of the said cement. But the customs authority does not clear the goods raising objections as to procedural matters. What is the remedy of the respondent in such a case?</u>

<u>The answer is provided in the Import Policy Order, 1989-91 to which reference has been made by the learned Additional Attorney-General for a different purpose. Clause 18 of the said Order provides for "Miscellaneous provisions regarding imports" and Clause 18(4) reads thus;</u>

<u>4) Release of Goods Detained by the Customs: If a consignment of imported goods is detained by the Customs Authority the concerned importer may apply to the Chief Controller with prayer to issue release instruction to the Customs Authority for clearance of the consignment. Such an application shall be submitted to the Chief Controller within 90 (ninety) days from the date of objection given in writing by the Customs Authority. Applications submitted after the expiry of the above time limit will not be considered except in special cases. Such application must be accompanied by written objection (s) of the Customs Authority or detention Memo showing the ground (s) for detention of the consignment. The Chief Controller shall for dispensation of justice expeditiously dispose of such cases with due consideration to the relevant issues.</u>

<u>33. The legal course for the respondent was, therefore, to approach the CCI & E who alone could issue release instruction to the Customs Authority. This the respondent does not seem to have done ever although it was moving from pillar to post. We are not satisfied with the argument that no clearance from the CCI & E was necessary, rather we are clearly of the opinion that not only a clearance from the Bangladesh Bank was necessary but a clearance from the CCI & E was very much necessary in the special facts of the present case. In any case, Bangladesh Bank made CCI & E's clearance a condition precedent for its own clearance. From the above discussion it is abundantly clear that the respondent had not had the necessary clearance from the relevant authorities and as such it cannot be said that the Customs Authority acted without jurisdiction in refusing clearance of the goods to the respondent.</u>

<u>34. Now to come back to the second instance as to the poor understanding of the relevant law by the High Court Division, reference may be made to pages 116-119 of the impugned judgment in the paper book. Upon quoting section 48 of the Customs Act it has been stated that the Collector of Customs is also empowered under the said section to direct the owner for production of documents and also to ask him question if any doubt arises in his mind while clearing the goods in question. It has been further stated:</u>

<u>"Therefore, after production of Bill of Lading by the present petitioner with the endorsement on the overleaf, the requirement of section 48 of the Act is also fulfilled. Therefore, there is hardly any impediment or obstruction to clear the goods by the petitioner. The Collector of Customs fortunately without delivering the goods to the petitioner exceeded his power in proceeding to hold auction sale of the goods in question although the petitioner is always diligent and keen in clearing the goods from the Customs Authorities."</u>

<u>35. The learned Judges, we are very sorry to say, had been casual enough as even not to notice that under section 48 it is not the owner of the goods but the person-in-charge of a conveyance or his duly authorised agent who is required to deliver to the appropriate officer the bill of lading and other documents in respect of the conveyance after the presentation of the import manifest. Section occurs in Chapter VII under the Heading "Arrival and Departure of Conveyance." The provisions of the said Chapter relate to arrival of a conveyance, delivery of import manifest in respect of a vessel or conveyance and allied matters in respect to the same. The owner of the goods comes into the picture under Chapter IX as already noticed after the discharge or removal of the cargo from the vessel or the Conveyance, as the case may be is done. We make no secret of our concern and dismay with the careless manner and application in which the impugned judgment has been delivered. The learned counsel for the respondent did not mince matters in disowning the same in the judgment which he came to support.</u>

<u>36. As to the powers of the Customs Authority to put the disputed cement to auction sale the consideration becomes only academic when it is found that the respondent was not entitled to claim the clearance of the same and the Customs Authorities were within their rights to refuse clearance to it. The appellants, however, stated in their affidavit-in opposition that the Customs Authority had to take steps for disposal of the consignment through auction when the importer M/s MA Baker failed to clear the goods on payment of duties and charges within the stipulated time as envisaged in section 82 of the Customs Act and due notice to the owner was also given before such auction sale as cement is perishable in nature and significant portion of the consignment had already undergone deterioration and damage due to delay and defective packing and some of the cement bags were already torn and had to be repacked and this will show the extent of damage of the consignment. In order to safeguard the Government revenue interest the collector had to take quick steps under section 82, it was further stated. These assertions have remained unchallenged. The holding of auction of the disputed cement was, therefore, fully justified.</u>

37. In view of the discussion above, we hold that the High Court Division was wholly wrong in finding that the Collector of Customs acted without lawful authority in refusing to deliver the cement in question to the respondent No. 1 and in holding the auction sale thereof. The result, therefore, is that the appeals are allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment is set aside.

Mustafa Kamal J : I have had advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers ATM Afzal and Latifur Rahman JJ I concur with the decision of ATM Afzal J

Latifur Rahman J : I have had the advantage of reading before hand the judgment just delivered by my learned brother ATM Afzal J. I find it difficult to agree with the judgment as I find that the Collector of Customs, Chittagong most arbitrarily and illegally refused to delver the balance quantity of cement validly and lawfully imported in Bangladesh to its owner, respondent No.1, Anis & Co. and illegally sold the same in auction under section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969.

40. Since, ATM Afzal J has elaborately written the case of all the parties before us, I need not repeat the same again.

41. The High Court Division by the impugned judgment having made the Rule absolute, the Government and the Board of Revenue filed the leave petition seeking leave to appeal. Leave was granted to consider whether the auction sale of the balance consignments of cement by the Collector of Customs, Chittagong was lawfully held under section 82 of the Customs Act in the facts and circumstances of the present case; that when M/s Anis & Co. submitted the original bill of lading duly endorsed in its favour by Transclear, the consignee of the importer, could the Collector of Customs, Chittagong lawfully refuse to deliver the balance quantity of cement to Anis & Co. when admittedly the cement was validly and lawfully imported into Bangladesh and that whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division have decided a disputed question of title in respect of balance quantity of cement in writ jurisdiction.

42. In this case, there are certain admitted and undisputed facts which need be referred here first to understand the plea of refusal by the Collector of Customs, Chittagong not to hand over the balance quantity of imported cement to Anis &Co. who claimed ownership of the same.

(l) It is admitted by the appellants and the respondents that M/s MA Baker was the original importer of the consignments of cement and the import of the cement was validly and lawfully made by M/s MA Baker by opening irrevocable letter of credit No. 1502/2518/90 and LCA No.6/1502 dated 11.7.90 for importation of the cement in question. It appears that cement is a freely importable item, which is neither a banned nor a restricted item and for importation of the cement no permit of the office of the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports was necessary. The import of cement can be made freely by opening a letter of credit and in the form prescribed for the authorisation of the opening of the L/C without obtaining import licence. Thus, it appears that valid importation of 10000 metric tons of cement was not in dispute. As a matter of fact, after the arrival of the consignments of cement the original importer M/s MA Baker who could not produce the original bill of lading was allowed to take 4000 metric tons of cement on furnishing indemnity bond. Admittedly, 5 bills of Entry were submitted under section 79 of the Customs Act for clearance of 10 consignments of cement and all those bills of entry were duly assessed by the appropriate officer of the Customs House, Chittagong. But the balance consignments remained uncleared as Customs Duties and other charges remained unpaid. The delivery of 4000 metric tons of cement to M/s MA Baker also prima facie shows that no objection was raised from the Collector of Customs with regard to the validity and invalidity of the importation of the cement, otherwise the same also could not nave been handed over to M/s MA Baker, the importer.

(2) It is admitted that Transclear was the consignee of M/s MA Baker and it is also not disputed that the bill of lading was althrough lying with 'Transclear'. The bills of lading show consignee "order of Transclear", whereas the importer M/s MA Baker has been designated as "notifying party".

(3) Admittedly, the non-negotiable copy of the bill of lading was submitted by M/s MA Baker duly certified by the LC opening Bank, Grindlays Bank, Chittagong for Customs assessment as the original bill of lading was not received by the importer. It may be mentioned here that the practice of issuing a set of three original bills of lading is very ancient in International Contracts of Sale. Of the Bills of lading there was commonly three bills of one tenor. One of them was given to the ship (MV Banglar Kiron); another bill was sent to the party to whom the goods were consigned (M/s MA Baker); the third remained with the Merchant (Transclear) for his testimony against the master, and for protection of the interest of Transclear in case it becomes necessary.

(4) Admittedly, M/s MA Baker never appeared in the picture after taking delivery of 4000 metric tons of cement and nobody claimed the balance quantity of cement other than respondent No. 1 with original Bills of lading duly " endorsed in full" in his favour by name the consignee, Transclear.

(5) Admittedly, the transaction in the present case is "cash against document" which is an internationally recognised business practice. The said transaction was not denied by the appellants and which is also permissible under the Import Policy of the Government of Bangladesh.

43. Keeping these above admitted facts in view, I am now to consider the claim of Anis & Co. as the owner of the cement, and the refusal of the Customs Authority to deliver the cement and to hold auction of the cement under section 82 of the Customs Act. It appears that when Anis & Co. claimed the balance quantity of cement on the basis of ownership by virtue of bills of lading validly endorsed in his favour by Transclear, the Customs Authority refused to return the cement to Anis & Co. by holding that the import of cement having been made by M/s MA Baker, Anis & Co. could not be admitted as importer and the Customs Authority refused to deliver the cement. It is on record that all the shipping documents namely, invoice, Bill of lading, Policy of Insurance, LC. Authorisation Form and all other connected papers for the importation of the cement were duly filed before the Customs Authority at Chittagong by the Importer. The Customs Authority constantly raised the objection that Anis & Co. was not the importer. This was nobody's case that Anis & Co. was the importer. Admittedly M/s MA Baker was the importer. Anis & Co. only claimed the balance quantity of cement on the basis of the bill of lading claiming his ownership in the cement. In such circumstances, the plea taken by the Customs Authority that Anis & Co. was not the importer was really difficult to understand. The importer submitted all documents before the Customs Authority for clearance of all consignments of cement.

<u>44. From the tenor of objection raised by the Customs Authority in their letters dated 13.12.90 and 23.12.90, it appears that they wanted to reject the claim of ownership of Anis & Co. on the plea that he was not the importer. In the instant case there could not be two importers, as M/s MA Baker had already imported the cement by opening valid irrevocable LC and observing other legal formalities. This objection of the Customs Authority of rejecting the claim of respondent No.1 and directing him to produce all relevant documents regarding importation of the cement was indeed difficult for me to understand, when as a matter of fact all shipping documents were produced earlier by the Importer himself before the Customs Authority. I fail to understand from where the owner can again procure necessary papers showing re-importation of the goods when already the documents relating to valid import in the present case were lying before the Customs Authority. The Collector of Customs refused to deliver the balance quantity of cement to Anis & Co. primarily on the ground that he was not the Importer. In the Customs Act, 1969 importer has not been defined any where. I may mention here, that section 79 of the Customs Act which deals with entry for home consumption or warehousing speaks of submitting the bill of entry by the owner of any imported goods. This section does not speak of importer. Section 80 of the Customs Act which deals with assessment of duty, speaks of imported goods and the owner of such goods. Section 82 of the Customs Act speaks of procedure in case of goods not cleared or warehoused or transhipped after unloading within a specified period. This section clearly indicates that if any goods are not cleared or warehoused or transhipped within a specified period then the appropriate officer, after due notice to the owner, can sell the goods. Section 83 of the Customs Act reads as follows:</u>

<u>"83. Clearance for home-consumption.- When the owner of any goods entered for home-consumption and assessed under section 80 has paid the import duty and other charges, if any in respect of the same, the appropriate officer, if he is satisfied that the import of the goods is not prohibited or in breach of any restrictions or conditions applying to the import of such goods, may make an order for the clearance of the same;"</u>

45. The relevant sections of Chapter IX of the Customs Act which speak of discharge of cargo and entry inwards of goods no where speak of importer but those sections speak of "owner." Hence, it is dear that either the importer or the owner of the goods can file the bill of entry for the assessment of customs duties and taxes and for clearance of the goods. In view of the fact, that original bills of lading were submitted by Anis & Co. at a subsequent point of time when the original importer never came to lift the cement after full customs assessment, the question of ownership of the cement became very relevant for the Customs Authority to consider in this case as per the sections mentioned above. Section 83 of the Customs Act clearly speaks that the appropriate officer, if satisfied that the import of the goods is not prohibited or in breach of any restrictions or conditions applying to the import of such goods, he may make an order for the clearance of the same to the owner. In the present case, I have already indicated above that cement is a freely importable item for which no import permit or permission of the Government is required.

46. Anis & So was not claiming as importer. But its claim in the balance quantity of cement was as an owner on the basis of bills of lading" endorsed in full" in its name by the consignee. In International Mercantile Law a Bill of lading answers three purposes:

(a) It is a receipt for the goods shipped, containing the terms on which they have been received.

(b) It is evidence of the contract for the carriage of goods.

(c) It is a document of title to the goods specified therein.

47. Thus, I am to see whether on the basis of the bills of lading, Anis & Co. could lawfully claim the possession of the cement as owner of the same. From the original bills of lading it is found that those were "endorsed in full" in favour of Anis & Co. and by virtue of those endorsements under the Mercantile Customs and Practice Anis & Co. as a transferee from the consignee Transclear got a valid and legal title in the cement in question. The copy of the bill of lading which was submitted to the Customs Authority was a non-negotiable copy and that was not a transferable bill of lading. But the bills of lading submitted by Anis & Co. were negotiable in Mercantile Customs and Practice. Further, from the bills of lading, I find that there is "full endorsement" in addition to the endorser's signature, there is direction to deliver to Anis & Co. (specified person). Thus, in the present case by "full endorsement" there is clear intention to transfer the cement in question in favour of respondent No. 1 Strictly speaking, no person but the consignee, as in the present case, Transclear, Switzerland when the bill of lading is made. out in his name, could pass legal title to the cement by endorsement of the bill and its prima facie effect is to vest ownership to Anis & Co. The learned Additional Attorney-General has cited the celebrated decision in the case of J. Swell Vs. James Burdick reported in (1884) Law Report Volume-X Appeal Cases-74 to strengthen his argument that the bill of lading was not intended to be an absolute document of transfer of title and possession. I must say outright that this decision instead of helping the learned Additional Attorney-General, supports the contention raised by Mr. Syed Istiaque Ahmed, the learned Advocate for respondent No. 1. The cited decision is a case wherein the shipper took a loan of L-300 from the appellant-bank for sending some machinery from London to Poti in Black Sea, under bills of lading. Since the shipper took loan of the amount from the bank, it endorsed in blank the bill of lading in favour of the bank as security for the loan. On the above fact, it was held by the learned Judges that the transaction by the bills of lading was intended by the parties to operate as a pledge only and not a transfer. In that decision it was held that the endorsement in blank of the bills of lading to the bank as security for loan did not transfer the property in the goods to the bank. In that decision it was unequivocally held that the property in the goods did not pass unless it is intended by the contract that it shall pass. In that decision Earl of Selbourne LC has beautifully expressed the meaning of endorsement of the bill of lading in the following language:

"The facts here are simply an endorsement in blank and deposit of the bills of lading, so endorsed, by way of security for money advanced. There are no special circumstances, except that the endorsee never did obtain, and that it was never possible for him (in fact) to obtain, delivery of goods."

48. Thus, in the fact of that case, the bills of lading were only a document of pledge and it was not a sale out and out and by assignment of the bill of lading the whole legal title to the goods never passed. The decision in that case has made it clear that the effect to the endorsement of a bill of lading depends entirely on the particular circumstances of each endorsement.

49. In this case there is another aspect which will be relevant for understanding the nature of transaction as is understood in International Contracts of Sale. M/s Transclear purchased the cement from an Iraqi Trading Company and sold the same to M/s Nidera for "cash against documents" and Nidera sold the same to M/s MA Baker of Chittagong. In a CIF and C & F Contract, it is a contract for sale of document rather than sale of goods. In normal C & F Contract, as in this case, the property of the goods passed to Anis & Co. upon transfer of the document (bills of lading). The contract was fully performed by the delivery of relevant bills of lading endorsed in full. It is generally understood that under a CIF and C & F Contract, "cash against document" the price is due upon, or within a reasonable time after tender of the documents, irrespective of the arrival of the ship and notwithstanding that the buyer had no opportunity of inspecting the goods to ascertain whether they are in accordance with contract. Thus, it is apparent that the transaction of the original supplier "Transclear" and the transferee "Nidera" being one of "cash against document," in the bill of lading Transclear had been recorded as consignee, and the undelivered cement could be resold by the supplier Nidera or Transclear while cement remained undelivered.

<u>50. In this judgment, I have very elaborately dealt with the International Mercantile Practice and usage as because this case involves import of cement from a foreign land by a local importer from Foreign Merchant by opening irrevocable letter of credit. It is necessary to understand the nature of transaction and its bearing on the question of refusal by the Customs Authority in delivering the imported cement to its owner who is a valid endorsee in full and who under law and equity is entitled to the possession of the same. I may, however, say that Customs Authority nowhere in their correspondences with Anis & Co. raised any objection with regard to title/possession of the cement. Since, Anis & Co. was claiming the balance quantity of cement as owner, the customs authority was under a legal obligation under the statute to decide this aspect, as all the relevant sections of Chapter IX of the Customs Act deal with imported goods and the owner thereof.</u>

<u>51. To understand the objections of the Customs Authority in not handing over imported balance quantity of cement to Anis & Co. suffice it to refer to some letters. It is on record that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation on 16.10.90 wrote a letter to the Bangladesh Bank intimating that the importer M/s MA Baker only took delivery of 4000 metric tons of cement on furnishing indemnity bond issued by the Grindlays Bank. In that letter they further requested the Bangladesh Bank not to allow any party to lift the balance quantity of cement. In view of this, respondent No. 1's Banker Agrani Bank applied for permission for remittance of USS 1,25,000.00. In reply the Bangladesh Bank by their letter dated 22.11.90 intimated that the clearance of the imported cement by Anis & Co. is not in keeping with the general conditions of Import Policy Order and as such the permission of Chief Controller of Imports and Exports was necessary. In the said letter the Bangladesh Bank proposed to consider the question of remittance of foreign exchange in favour of Transclear of Switzerland on some conditions, namely-(1) Anis & Co. would obtain permission of the CCI & E, (2) Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, Customs Authority and Port Authority would give no objection, (3) There would be no dispute in any Court, (4) After satisfying the demands of Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and Chittagong Port Authority USS 1,25,000.00 would be remitted in Foreign Exchange to be acquired from wage-earner market and (5) Attested copies of Bill of Entries of the Customs Authority are to be produced.</u>

<u>The letter further shows that after complying with all the above formalities, Bangladesh Bank could be again approached for remittance of the money. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 1 submitted that from the facts of the case, admittedly some of the conditions imposed in the letter were either honest in law and fact or others were already fulfilled. Hence this letter may in reality be construed as an accord of permission for remittance of foreign exchange by the Bangladesh Bank. In support of his submission he submitted that the permission of CCI & E was not necessary in view of the letter of the Ministry of Commerce dated 2.12.90, which is the parent Ministry of CCI & E. This letter clearly indicates that no permission of the Government is necessary for import of cement other than general conditions as mentioned in the import Policy Order, 1989-91. Hence, he submitted that the first condition that was referred in the letter of the Bangladesh Bank was not lawfully necessary at all. It is also found from the record that there was no claim either of Bangladesh Shipping Corporation or of Port Authority and that there was no court case pending. Further, the attested copies of the bills of entry duly assessed were lying before the Customs Authority for payment of customs dues and taxes and for clearance of the goods. I really find that some conditions were non-existent and some were already fulfilled by that time. Thus. I hold that Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed is correct in his submission, as I find substantial and lawful compliance of all conditions made in the letter dated 22.11.90. It will be profitable to refer to the letters of the Customs Authority dated 13.12.90 and the impugned letter dated 23.12.90. In the letter dated 13.12.90, the Customs Authority mentioned that Anis & Co. was not the importer; that the conditions of Import Policy Order, 1989-91 were not followed and that the permission of CCI & E and Bangladesh Bank had not been obtained. It appears that the Customs Authority by their two letters unnecessarily raised a plea that the import of cement in the present case was not done in accordance with general conditions of Import Policy Order, 1989-91. In none of those letters the Customs Authority clearly pointed out what specific conditions were not followed in the instant case. I have gone through the entire Import Policy Order, 1989-91 from where it appears that in case of freely importable item like cement, only letter of credit and L/C Authorisation form is required and no import licence is required from the Government. Apart from this, there is no other specific condition that is to be followed by the importer in importing freely importable items. Hence, this objection is totally vague and not sustainable in law. I, for myself, could not lay my hands on any specific condition other than those mentioned above. It may be pointed out here, that Import Policy Order, 1989-91, clause 18(4), speaks of release of goods detained by the Customs Authority. This clause speaks that if a consignment of imported goods is detained by the Customs Authority the concerned importer may apply to the Chief Controller with a prayer to issue release instructions to the Customs Authority for clearance of the consignment. Such application is to be filed within 90 days from the date of the objection given in writing by Customs Authority. In the present case, admittedly, the importer took some consignments of cement and never came to lift the balance quantity of cement. Anis & Co. being not the importer it could not file the application. Further, it is on record that Ministry of Commerce by their letter dated 2.12.90 clearly replied to the query of Anis & Co. that no permission of the Government was necessary. This clause relates to the importer only and in fact the importer was allowed to take ie cement This fact also shows that when the Customs Authority allowed the importer to lift the cement there could be no lawful objection with regard to the importation of cement as per Import Policy Order, 1989-91 and lifting of the rest quantity of cement by respondent No. 1. Consequently, I hold that no permission from CCI & E was necessary in the instant cases. This objection with regard to Import Policy Order, 1989-91 was made by the Collector of Customs most illegally and whimsically in this case without any application of judicial mind to the relevant law and fact.</u>

52. In the ultimate analysis, the Collector of Customs was acting under the provision of the Customs Act, and hence I am to see whether the order of refusal to deliver the cement to the owner was lawfully passed and whether the auction of the said cement was lawfully held under section 82 of the Customs Act. The statute empowers the Collector of Customs to auction sale the goods if the same is not cleared by the owner within a specified time after due notice to the owner. It may be mentioned that section 82 of the Customs Act provides that due notice is to be given to the owner. In the present case the owner was making all frantic efforts to get release of the goods from Customs Authority after paying customs duties and taxes. The Collector of Customs instead of releasing the goods as claimed by Anis & Co. put the same in auction to the prejudice of respondent No.1. This is not only illegal but not authoriscd under section 82 of the Customs Act. Reading the section as a whole it appears to me that the question of auction sale comes under this section when the goods are not cleared after unloading within a specified time by the owner. The manner in which the auction sale was held by raising all flimsy and irrelevant objection in spite of the claim of respondent No.1. is contrary to the spirit of this section. The law imposes a duty on the Customs Authority to act quasi-judicially and the authority having failed to discharge that duty the learned Judges of the High Court Division were correct to hold that the refusal order and consequent auction sale were illegal and not authorised by law. The Customs Authority failed to perform their statutory duty in this regard.

53. From the judgment of the High Court Division it further appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly proceeded that there having been valid and lawful import of the cement by M/s MA Baker the Customs Authority wrongly refused to deliver the balance quantity of cement to Anis & Co. In this regard. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that the Customs Authority though primarily invested with the power to levy and collect customs duties and taxes it can also inquire into the legality or illegality of the importation or exportation of any goods in the country: But he argued that in the present case there was no illegal importation or any unauthorised trading of the cement and the interest of the Government was fully protected in collection of customs duties.

<u>54. In the present case, admittedly, there being no dispute with regard to the ownership of the cement, the learned Judges of the High Court Division wrongly observed that the parties can decide the question of title in a Civil Court. This observation was not necessary. As a matter of fact, none including the Collector of Customs raised any objection as to the ownership of the cement of respondent No. 1. Thus on a careful consideration of the materials on record and the point involved in this case. I am of the view that the learned Judges of the High Court Division have rightly held that Anis &Co. is lawfully entitled to the cement in question and the Collector of Customs most illegally and arbitrarily refused to deliver the same to the rightful owner and illegally held the auction in an unauthorised manner not contemplated under the Customs Act.</u>

55. The Customs Act is a complete code in itself. It provides for all eventualities and exigencies such as imposition of customs duties and taxes. release of imported goods confiscation penalties imprisonment etc. In the present case there being no allegation that the import was illegal and unlawful from any agencies of Government, the Customs Authority acted illegally in raising unsubstantial and unlawful objections to the great prejudice and hardship of a citizen. The Customs Authority could not lawfully refuse to deliver the cement to its owner in the facts and circumstances of the present case. There being no non-observance of any provisions of the Customs Act, how could the imported goods be lawfully refused taking recourse to other objections concerning other laws by the Collector of Customs.

56. It may be pointed out that Import Policy Order. 1989-91 was promulgated in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950. Any contravention of any order made or deemed to have been made under this Act or the Rules provides for legal action by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports. In this case there is no such allegation at all. The law of Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 authorises the Bangladesh Bank to take legal actions for violation of Foreign Exchange Regulation. if there be any. In this case there is also no allegation of any violation as such. Thus. I hold that the learned Judges were correct in holding that the Customs Authority acted illegally and beyond the scope of the Customs Act.

57. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation after the arrival of the cement started legal proceedings in courts of law and failed in those cases. Thereafter it wrote letters to the Bangladesh Bank and to other agencies not to allow anybody to lift the cement. In such circumstances, respondent No. 1 had to move the Bangladesh Bank, the Chief Controller, Imports and Exports, Ministry of Commerce and the Board of Revenue to get his redress. Finally, respondent No. 1 brought the matter before the High Court in writ jurisdiction to get redress of his grievances.

In view of the discussions made above, I hold that the High Court Division was totally correct in holding that the Collector of Customs acted without lawful authority in refusing to deliver the cement in question to respondent No. 1 and in holding auction under section 82 of the Customs Act. Accordingly, these appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

Order of the Court

By majority decision the appeals are allowed without cost.

End.
